text: Every environment this course has built so far has been one-off: one resource group, one VNet. A real team runs dev, staging, and prod side by side, and copy-pasting the same resource block into each one creates a real maintenance problem — fix a rule in one copy, and it's easy to forget the other two. That's the problem a Terraform module solves, and it's worth understanding why before writing one.

Here's the naive version: an azurerm_virtual_network block duplicated across dev and staging, changing only the name and address space. It works, until someone decides every VNet needs a network security group attached, or a naming audit flags a mismatch — and that fix has to land in every copy by hand. It's the same copy-pasted-loop problem this path already covered on the PowerShell side, just one layer lower, inside the infrastructure itself.

A module gives a proven pattern — call it our standard VNet setup — one name and one home: a folder of .tf files that takes in a few inputs and produces the same resource every time, NSG and naming convention already baked in. Fix it once inside the module, and every environment calling it picks up the fix automatically, the same way a shared function means fixing one definition instead of three separate copies.

It's tempting to turn everything into a module from day one, but that's its own mistake — a module adds indirection, inputs to track and outputs to trace, that isn't worth paying for until real duplication exists. The practical rule: once the same resource block has been copy-pasted two or three times, especially across environments or teams, extract it. Before that point, a plain resource block in the root configuration stays simpler to read.

A module isn't a special Terraform feature — it's just a folder of .tf files with its own input variables and outputs, called from a module block the same way a resource block configures a resource. Next lesson writes one in full: a real network module with vnet_name, address_space, and subnet_count as inputs, called from a root configuration.
